- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.6) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.3) or volatile, model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to account for risk premium or market panic.
- Model frequently overshoots after sharp price spikes (e.g., +5–10% in 1–2 days); apply a 2–5 day decay filter to smooth out overreaction.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., price drops after peak or rises after trough), model often fails to adjust; apply a 3–5 day moving average to align with recent trend.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to be too optimistic in early periods (e.g., first 5–7 days); reduce forecast by 2–5% for first 5 days if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “0.00” or extreme lows, model often misses downward momentum; add a 1–3% downward bias to forecast if sentiment is flat or negative.
- When sentiment is high but price is falling, model may ignore sentiment; adjust forecast downward by 1–2% if sentiment >0.7 but price is trending down.
